L857: ## Abstract
L858: 
L859: Study Objectives
L860: 
L861: Since genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of sleep phenotypes have been conducted in differing populations and definitions of sleep phenotypes vary across studies, we investigated associations between several polygenic risk scores (PRSs) and potential sleep definitions among multiethnic cohorts.
L862: 
L863: Materials and Methods
L864: Using data from four cohorts (HCHS/SOL, ARIC, MESA, BHS, N = 16 895), we considered multiple definitions of short and long sleep, insomnia, and excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS). Polygenic risk scores (PRSs) were developed based on summary statistics from GWAS in European ancestry individuals from the UK Biobank (UKB) and from GWAS conducted in a multiethnic population from the Million Veteran Program (MVP).
L865: Study-specific analyses estimated associations between sleep PRSs and corresponding sleep measures per 1 standard deviation increase in the PRS. Models were adjusted for age, sex, ancestral principal components, and center and race as appropriate. Results were meta-analyzed across studies.
L866: Results
L867: PRSs based on European ancestry UKB GWAS had statistically significant associations with multiple definitions of the corresponding sleep phenotypes.
L868: Associations that were most consistent across studies included: short sleep PRS with ≤6 hours (OR = 1.23, p = 1.80x10^{-7}, p_{het} = 0.97); long sleep PRS with ≥9 hours (OR = 1.09, p = 6.76x10^{-4}, p_{het} = 0.77); insomnia PRS with the Women’s Health Initiative Insomnia Rating Scale (WHIIRS) ≥10 or a subset of three questions ≥6 in ARIC (OR = 1.17, p = 5.51x10^{-10}, p_{het} = 0.69); and EDS PRS with Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) ≥11 (OR = 1.23, p = 1.83x10^{-13}, p_{het} = 0.83).
L869: PRSs based on multi-ancestry MVP GWAS had weaker associations compared to those based on European ancestry only.
L870: Conclusions
L871: 
L872: By evaluating several types of sleep PRSs and sleep phenotypes, we were able to highlight which sleep PRS performed well across diverse populations and which sleep definitions better captured genetic underpinnings.

L881: Statement of Significance
L882: Sleep disorders are associated with a variety of health outcomes, including cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and Alzheimer’s disease. Previous studies have identified numerous genetic variants associated with short and long sleep durations, insomnia and excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS), from which summary measures called polygenic risk scores (PRSs) have been developed. However, previous genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have been conducted in differing populations.
L883: Further, information on sleep is often self-reported via questionnaire and specific questions can vary across studies. Therefore, we sought to evaluate associations between multiple sleep PRSs and a variety of sleep definitions utilizing data from over 16 000 individuals from four cohort studies (HCHS/SOL, MESA ARIC, and BHS).
L884: In conjunction with demographic and environmental information, this analysis can help inform which sleep PRSs and sleep definitions to prioritize in future studies, especially for cross-study collaborations.
L885: ## Introduction
L886: Approximately half of adults aged 55–85 years in the United States are estimated to have symptoms of a sleep disorder or disturbance, such as short and long sleep durations, insomnia or excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) [1]. Sleep disorders are associated with a variety of cardiovascular- and age-related outcomes, including hypertension, myocardial infarction, stroke, diabetes, obesity, depression, and Alzheimer’s disease [1,2].
L887: Despite the important role of sleep in the development of cardiovascular diseases and adverse cognitive aging, sleep disorders are not widely targeted in health interventions. This is likely in part because the biological mechanisms underlying the associations between sleep and chronic conditions are not fully understood. In addition, heterogeneity in characterizing sleep disorders across studies can hinder comprehensive assessment.
L888: While polysomnography reliably measures many parameters of sleep, it does not capture all of its aspects [3,4]. It can also be cost and time prohibitive on a large-scale [3,4]. Often large cohort studies rely on self-reported sleep measures obtained from questionnaires to capture the multifactorial nature of sleep as well as the subjective perception of sleep [3,4]. However, sleep-related questions and their potential responses may vary between studies [3,4].
